english: I'm jealous / I envy you (the nice kind)
usage: Polite; the everyday warm way to say you wish you had what someone has
반말, said freely to a friend
Half-to-yourself exclamation; the most natural spoken form, even around elders
완전 ('totally') boosts the warmth — common in chat messages
examples: A: 다음 주에 제주도 가요! / B: 와, 진짜요? 부러워요!
A: I'm going to Jeju next week! / B: Wow, really? I'm so jealous!
A/B exchange showing the natural warm reaction to good news; 진짜요? adds genuine surprise
A: 집이 회사랑 걸어서 5분이에요. / B: 아… 너무 부럽다.
A: My place is five minutes' walk from work. / B: Ahh… I'm so jealous.
반말 mutter 부럽다 as pure wistful reaction — the most natural everyday form
휴가 간다고요? 진짜 부러워요. 저는 방학이 없어서요.
You're going on vacation? I'm really jealous — I don't get time off.
Adding your own situation (저는 방학이 없어서요) makes the envy sound sincere, not bitter
nuance: 부러워요 comes from the adjective 부럽다 ('to be envious'), and it captures the GOOD, warm kind of envy — 'lucky you, I wish that were me.' Koreans say it constantly as a friendly compliment on good news: a trip, a new phone, a five-minute commute. It is never hostile. Keep it far from 질투 / 질투하다 ('jealousy'), which is the dark, possessive jealousy of a romantic rival or someone who resents your success — saying 질투나요 to a friend's vacation news sounds creepy or bitter, so 부러워요 is the safe everyday choice. For register: 부러워요 is polite, 부러워 is 반말, and 부럽다 is the bare adjective exclamation Koreans mutter even around elders — because the plain-form exclamatory 다 functions like thinking aloud rather than 반말 aimed at someone. The number-one English-speaker pitfall is the particle and direction: you do NOT say 당신을 부러워요 ('I envy YOU' with an object) — mark what is envied with 이/가 (가방이 부러워요 'I envy your bag', 네가 부러워 'I envy you/your situation'), or simply say 부러워요 about the whole thing. A look-alike trap: 부럽다 ('envious') vs. 부끄럽다 ('shy/embarrassed') — they share 부 but are opposite-feeling words.

structuredNuance.t: 직역 would be 'I am envious.' But in practice 부러워요 functions as a warm COMPLIMENT — 'lucky you, I wish that were me' — not a statement of bitterness. The feeling is openly shared and affectionate, not hidden or hostile.

Use freely to friends, family, coworkers of similar rank, even casual strangers, whenever you hear good news — a trip, a deal, a short commute. It is the natural warm reaction. 부러워요 is polite-casual; 부러워 is 반말; 부럽다 works as an exclamation even around seniors. Avoid it only when the context is competitive or you're already tense with someone (there 질투 might apply).

vs. 질투(나다): 질투 is dark, possessive jealousy — the resentment of a love rival. Saying 질투나요 to a friend's good news sounds hostile. vs. 부끄럽다: looks similar (부) but means 'shy/embarrassed' — completely different. 부러워요 = warm envy; 부끄러워요 = I'm embarrassed. Keep them separate.

완전 부러워요 ('totally jealous'), 진짜 부러워요 ('really jealous'), 부럽네요 (soft polite observation, '~must say I envy you'), 부러우면 지는 거예요 (joke: 'if you're jealous, you lose'). Name the envied thing with 이/가: 네 휴가가 부러워요.

Do NOT mark the person with 을/를: 너를 부러워요 is wrong. The envied thing/situation takes 이/가: 네가 부러워, 그 가방이 부러워요. Also don't confuse 부럽다 ('envious') with 부끄럽다 ('embarrassed') — they sound alike but mean opposite things.

mistakes: Saying 질투나요 to react to a friend's good news.
질투 is dark, possessive jealousy (a love rival, resentment). Friendly 'lucky you' envy is 부러워요. 질투나요 to a friend's vacation sounds hostile, not warm.
Marking the person as an object: 너를 부러워.
부럽다 takes the envied thing/situation with 이/가, not a person with 을/를. Say 네가 부러워 ('I envy you/your situation') or just 부러워.
Translating 'I'm jealous OF your car' as 차에 부러워요.
Don't use 에. The envied thing takes 이/가: 차가 부러워요, or simply 부러워요 about the whole thing.

usage: Polite-casual; about a situation, NOT usually said directly at the person causing it
반말, to a close friend or muttered to yourself when frustrated
It's driving me crazy with irritation
-아 죽겠어요 ('to death') maxes out the frustration for comic effect
네요 turns it into a shared grumble rather than a complaint aimed at someone
examples: A: 와이파이 또 끊겼어? / B: 응, 아 진짜 짜증나.
A: Did the WiFi cut out again? / B: Yeah, ugh, this is so annoying.
A/B exchange; the friends vent together about a situation — not a person
버스가 또 안 와요. 짜증나요.
The bus isn't coming again. So annoying.
Venting about a frustrating situation; natural because the irritation targets the bus, not a person
계속 같은 거 물어봐서 좀 짜증났어요.
They kept asking the same thing, so I got a bit irritated.
Past tense 짜증났어요 reports the irritation after the fact; 좀 softens it into a grumble rather than an accusation
nuance: 짜증나요 is from 짜증(이) 나다 ('irritation arises') — a verb built on the noun 짜증 ('irritation, annoyance'). It is the everyday word for the prickly, fed-up feeling when small things go wrong: the bus is late, the wifi drops, someone nags you for the fifth time. The word is honest and extremely common, but it is BLUNT, even slightly crude, so the safe zone is venting about a SITUATION to a friend, or muttering to yourself. Saying 짜증나요 straight to a person's face — especially a senior, a coworker, or staff — is confrontational, like snapping 'you're pissing me off.' For a controlled, polite complaint, soften with 좀 짜증나네요 or step up to 불편해요 ('it's uncomfortable/inconvenient') in formal contexts. The phrase people confuse it with is 화나요 ('I'm angry'): 화나다 is real, bigger outward anger, while 짜증나다 is petty irritation — using 화나요 for a late bus overstates it, and using 짜증나요 for a serious betrayal understates it. The grammar trap: 짜증(이) 나다 is intransitive, so you say 짜증나요 (irritation arises in you), never 짜증해요 (no such verb). Mark the cause with 때문에: 너 때문에 짜증나 ('I'm annoyed because of you') — still 반말-only and pointed.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: '짜증(irritation) 나다(arises)' — irritation wells up inside you. The real meaning is a caught-in-traffic, low-boil prickling irritation, not rage. It is situational and fleeting, not a judgment of character.

Use to vent about a situation to close friends or yourself — a late bus, a slow server, repeated interruptions. DO NOT say it to the face of a stranger, a senior, or someone serving you. That registers as 'you're annoying me' and causes a scene. With seniors, use 좀 불편하네요 or describe the problem calmly.

vs. 화나요: 화나다 is real, bigger anger directed at someone — using it for a late bus is overkill. vs. 불편해요: the polite alternative for formal complaints ('I'm a bit uncomfortable with this'). vs. 답답해요: the stuck, suffocating frustration (can't get through, not just annoyed). 짜증나다 = petty prickle; 화나다 = real anger; 답답하다 = boxed-in helplessness.
짜증 나 죽겠어요 (maxed-out, comic), 좀 짜증나네요 (softened shared grumble), 짜증났어요 (past tense report), 짜증 나게 하다 (causative — 'make someone irritated'). The irritation source takes 때문에: 너 때문에 짜증나.

짜증하다 does not exist — it's 짜증(이) 나다. Also do NOT say it directly to a person's face in a non-close relationship; this is a venting word for situations and close friends. Saying 화나요 for every 'upset' feeling misses the lighter, pricklier 짜증 register entirely.

mistakes: Saying 짜증나요 directly to staff or a senior.
It's blunt and confrontational, like 'you're annoying me.' For a polite complaint use 좀 불편해요 or describe the problem; save 짜증나 for friends/yourself.
Saying 짜증해요.
There is no verb 짜증하다. It's 짜증(이) 나다 — the irritation 'arises': 짜증나요. The 나다 part is essential.
Using 화나요 for minor annoyances.
화나다 is genuine anger; for a late bus or slow wifi it's overkill. The right word for petty irritation is 짜증나요.

usage: My heart's fluttering / I'm so giddy
Polite; the sweet, hopeful, butterflies-in-the-stomach excitement
Plain-form exclamation muttered to yourself; very natural
I'm so giddy / I can barely stand it
너무 ('so/too') amps the flutter into an almost-overwhelming sweetness
examples: A: 내일 첫 데이트잖아요! / B: 알아요, 어떡하지… 너무 설레요.
A: Tomorrow's your first date! / B: I know, oh man… I'm so nervous-excited.
A/B exchange showing the sweet romantic flutter; -잖아요 = 'you know, right?' and 어떡하지 expresses flustered delight
새 학기라 설레면서도 좀 떨려요.
It's a new semester, so I'm excited but also a little nervous.
Pairing 설레다 (pleasant flutter) with 떨리다 (nervous trembling) shows the real mix most people feel
첫눈이 왔어요. 왠지 설레네요.
The first snow fell. Somehow my heart's fluttering.
설레다 for a seasonal moment, not romance — shows how broadly Koreans use this word
nuance: 설레요 comes from 설레다 ('to flutter, to feel one's heart race with sweet anticipation'). This is the warm, hopeful, butterflies-in-the-stomach excitement — before a trip, a date, a reunion, the first snow. It is gentle, inward, and romantic-leaning, and Koreans use it constantly in everyday life and all over song lyrics and dramas. The crucial contrast is with 떨리다 ('to tremble / be nervous'): 떨리다 is the JITTERY nerves before an exam or a speech (can be bad nerves), while 설레다 is the PLEASANT flutter you actively welcome — they overlap (a first date is often both), but if you say 설레요 before a scary job interview it sounds strange, because 설레다 implies you're looking forward to it rather than dreading it. A cooler near-word is 기대돼요 ('I'm looking forward to it') — that is more mental and measured, while 설레다 is the physical, heart-fluttering sensation. Register: 설레요 is polite; 설레 is 반말; 설렌다 is the natural self-exclamation. The English-speaker pitfall is spelling and conjugation: the stem is 설레-, so present is 설레요 and past is 설렜어요 — NOT 설레여요 (a very common wrong form) and NOT 설래요 (equally common misspelling). Also it's intransitive: 마음이 설레요 ('my heart flutters'), you do not do 설레 to an object.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 설레다 = 'to flutter.' The real meaning is a sweet, whole-body flutter of anticipation — something you actively welcome, not a neutral tremble. Koreans use it for romantic feelings, seasons changing, travel, and any warm hopeful moment.

Use freely with anyone — friends, family, even in polite conversation, because the feeling is positive and warm. 설레요 (polite), 설레 (반말), 설렌다 (self-exclamation). It fits any happy anticipation: trips, romance, gifts, new seasons. Don't use it for something you dread — that signals a misread of the situation.

vs. 떨리다: 'to tremble/be nervous' — can be good OR bad nerves. 설레다 is always the happy flutter. A first date might be both (설레고 떨려요). vs. 기대돼요: 'I'm looking forward to it' — cooler, more mental. 설레다 is the physical heart-race. vs. 신나요: pumped/hyped energy. 설레다 is quieter and more inward.
너무 설레요, 설레서 잠이 안 와요 ('I'm so giddy I can't sleep'), 마음이 설레요 (명시적 subject), 설레는 마음으로 ('with a fluttering heart' — common in messages/cards). Past: 설렜어요.

Two traps: (1) misspelling — it's 설레요 / 설렜어요, NOT 설래요 or 설레여요; the stem is 설레-, a clean ㅔ-ending verb. (2) using 설레요 before something you dread — 설레다 implies you welcome it, so it sounds incongruous before a scary interview.

mistakes: Writing or saying 설레여요 / 설래요.
The stem is 설레-, so present is 설레요 and past is 설렜어요. 설레여요 and 설래요 are common but wrong; lock in 설레요.
Using 설레요 before something you dread (exam, scary interview).
설레다 implies happy anticipation. For nervous jitters use 떨려요 ('I'm nervous'). Mixing is fine only when you're genuinely excited too.
Treating it as 'excited' in the loud/hyped sense.
설레다 is a soft inner flutter, not pumped-up hype. For 'pumped/thrilled' loudness, 신나요 fits better; 설레다 is gentle anticipation.

usage: It's so embarrassing / I feel awkward
Polite; mild social embarrassment, lighter than mortification
반말, to a close friend after a small social slip
네요 shares the awkwardness softly, inviting a smile
-아 죽겠어요 maxes it for comic effect — for truly cringe moments
examples: 아, 민망해.
Ugh, how embarrassing.
Muttered after a small social slip-up — dropped something in public, said the wrong name
A: 발표하다가 말이 막혔어요. 어떡해요. / B: 아이고, 민망했겠다. 다들 이해해요.
A: I froze up mid-presentation. What do I do. / B: Oh no, that must've been so awkward. Everyone gets it.
A/B exchange using past 민망했겠다 ('you must have felt awkward') to empathize
칭찬을 너무 많이 받으니까 좀 민망하네요.
Getting so much praise makes me a bit bashful.
민망하다 for the squirmy feeling of over-the-top praise — not just a slip-up
nuance: 민망해요 (from 민망하다) is the squirmy, shrink-in-place embarrassment you feel after a small social misstep — you fell in public, got caught in a white lie, received too much praise, or an awkward silence dragged on. It is the 'oh no, this is so awkward, I want to disappear' feeling. Crucially, it is light and social — not deep shame or genuine mortification. The three-way contrast matters: 민망하다 = light awkward embarrassment; 부끄럽다 = shy/bashful blushing, also used for moral shame in formal writing; 창피하다 = mortified, 'I've lost face, I really screwed up publicly.' Many learners grab one word and overuse it — matching the strength is essential. If you froze during a presentation, 민망해요 or 창피해요 fits; if you're blushing at a compliment, 부끄러워요 or 민망해요; if you did something publicly shameful, 창피해요. Register: 민망해요 polite, 민망해 반말. The English-speaker pitfall is (1) defaulting to 부끄러워요 for every 'embarrassed' — a public trip or awkward moment is 민망해요, not the shy 부끄러워요; (2) confusing 민망하다 with 미안하다 ('sorry for an apology') — they sound similar to beginners but mean entirely different things. Also it's an adjective for your state: 민망해요, never 민망당했어요 or 민망나요.

structuredNuance.t: 민망하다 has no clean etymology hook for learners, but the feeling is clear: the squirmy, 'I want to shrink' social embarrassment after a minor misstep or too much attention. It is NOT shame about your character — it's social awkwardness.

민망해요 is polite-casual and appropriate in most registers. You can say it to a coworker ('아, 민망하네요') without it sounding unprofessional. It's softer and more relatable than 창피해요 in everyday speech. 민망해 is 반말; 민망하네요 is the most conversational polite form.

민망하다 = light awkward embarrassment (slip, pause, too much praise). 부끄럽다 = shy/blushing (modest shyness; formal moral shame). 창피하다 = mortified, lost face (real public screw-up). The strength order: 민망 < 창피 < 수치스럽다 (deep shame). Pick the level that fits the situation.
좀 민망하네요 (softened, shared), 민망해 죽겠어요 (comic max), 민망했겠다 (empathy past: 'you must have felt so awkward'), 민망한 상황 ('an awkward situation').

Two traps: (1) confusing 민망하다 with 미안하다 ('sorry for an apology') — they sound similar but mean opposite things: 민망해요 = 'I feel awkward,' 미안해요 = 'I'm sorry'; (2) reaching for 부끄러워요 for every 'embarrassed' — 부끄럽다 is shy/bashful, while 민망하다 fits awkward public slips better.

mistakes: Confusing 민망하다 with 미안하다.
They sound similar but 미안하다 = 'sorry (apology)', 민망하다 = 'awkward/embarrassed'. 'I feel awkward' is 민망해요, not 미안해요.
Using 부끄러워요 for an awkward public slip-up.
부끄럽다 leans 'shy/bashful.' A public fall or cringe moment is better 민망해요 (awkward) or 창피해요 (mortified). Pick the strength that fits.
Overshooting with 창피해요 for a tiny awkwardness.
창피하다 is strong 'humiliated/lost face.' For a small, harmless awkward moment, 민망해요 is the right, lighter word.

english: I feel proud and full (warm satisfaction)
usage: Polite; the warm glow of quiet accomplishment — humble and relatable
반말, shared with a friend after doing something well
Self-exclamation after completing something; often with a deep breath
I'm really proud / that really fills me
진짜 deepens the warm satisfaction without sounding boastful
examples: A: 드디어 3킬로 뺐어요! / B: 와, 진짜 뿌듯하겠다!
A: I finally lost three kilos! / B: Wow, you must feel so proud!
A/B exchange: 뿌듯하겠다 ('you must feel fulfilled') as a warm reaction to someone's achievement
애가 상 받는 거 보니까 너무 뿌듯했어요.
Seeing my kid get an award, I felt so proud.
뿌듯하다 for warm pride watching someone you love succeed — not just your own effort
한 달 동안 운동했더니 살이 빠져서 뿌듯해요.
After a month of exercise I lost weight, so I feel really fulfilled.
Pride in your own sustained effort paying off; -았더니 shows the result of that effort
nuance: 뿌듯해요 (from 뿌듯하다) is the warm, chest-swelling, quietly full satisfaction you feel when you (or someone you love) accomplished something — you finished a hard task, your kid did well, your effort paid off. The image is your chest swelling with happy fullness; it is INWARD and humble-feeling, which is why Koreans use it freely about themselves without sounding arrogant. The key contrast is with 자랑스럽다 ('to be proud of'): 자랑스럽다 is more outward, declarative pride you express ABOUT someone or something (아들이 자랑스러워요 'I'm proud of my son') — often directed at or about others. 뿌듯하다 describes the felt inner glow, usually for your own effort or a heartwarming moment you witnessed. Saying 제가 자랑스러워요 about yourself can sound boastful; saying 뿌듯해요 sounds modest and relatable — that is the crucial social difference. Don't confuse it with 만족하다 ('to be satisfied'), which is cooler, more evaluative, and less warm. Register: 뿌듯해요 polite, 뿌듯해 반말. Don't attach an object (뿌듯하다 is a state adjective): mark the cause with -아서/-니까 (끝내서 뿌듯해요).

structuredNuance.t: 직역: '뿌듯하다' means a full, swollen-feeling state — like your chest is pleasantly full. The real meaning is quiet, humble inner pride or satisfaction, not the public declaration 'I'm proud.' It is a feeling you have inside, not a performance for others.

Use freely with friends, family, coworkers — it never sounds arrogant because it describes a felt inner state, not a boast. You can say it after a personal achievement, a child's success, or a collective win. 뿌듯해요 is polite; 뿌듯해 is 반말. Even bosses/elders can hear it without it feeling off.

vs. 자랑스럽다: outward, declarative pride directed at someone/something — 아들이 자랑스러워요. Saying 제가 자랑스러워요 can sound boastful. 뿌듯해요 is the humble alternative for personal satisfaction. vs. 만족해요: cool, evaluative satisfaction ('it met the standard'). The warm, chest-filling feeling is 뿌듯해요.
진짜 뿌듯해요 (deeper satisfaction), 너무 뿌듯해요 ('so fulfilled'), 뿌듯하겠다 ('you must feel proud' — empathy form), 뿌듯했어요 (past tense, reporting after the fact). Cause takes -아서/-니까: 끝내서 뿌듯해요.

The pitfall is using 자랑스러워요 for personal warm-fuzzy satisfaction — that word signals outward pride and can sound boastful about yourself. When YOU feel the inner glow, say 뿌듯해요. Also don't attach an object: it's an adjective for your state, so mark the cause: 시험 끝나서 뿌듯해요, not 시험을 뿌듯해요.

mistakes: Saying 제가 자랑스러워요 for personal satisfaction.
자랑스럽다 is outward, declarative pride and can sound boastful about yourself. The humble inner glow is 뿌듯해요.
Attaching an object: 시험을 뿌듯해요.
뿌듯하다 describes your state, not a target. Mark the cause: 시험 끝나서 뿌듯해요 ('I feel fulfilled because the exam's over').
Swapping in 만족해요 for the warm feeling.
만족하다 is cool, evaluative 'satisfied (it met the standard).' The warm, chest-swelling pride is 뿌듯해요. They're not interchangeable.

english: I feel stifled / frustrated / boxed in
usage: Polite; the closed-in, can't-breathe-or-get-through feeling — physical OR emotional
반말, to a friend when you need to vent the boxed-in feeling
It's driving me up the wall (with stifled frustration)
-아 죽겠어요 maxes the stifled frustration — strong but commonly used among friends
Stronger idiom: '속(my insides) 터지다(burst)' — for the truly helpless, explosive pent-up feeling
examples: 방이 너무 좁아서 좀 답답해요.
The room is really small, so it feels a bit stifling.
Literal physical sense: cramped, stuffy, closed-in — not emotional at all
A: 어디가 힘들어요? / B: 말이 안 통해서 너무 답답해요.
A: What's been hard? / B: We can't communicate at all, so it's so frustrating.
A/B exchange showing the emotional sense: blocked, can't get through to someone
엄마가 제 말은 안 듣고 자기 말만 해서 답답해 죽겠어요.
Mom won't listen to me and only talks, so it's driving me crazy.
The classic stuck, can't-make-them-understand frustration; -만 ('only') sharpens the one-sided feel
nuance: 답답해요 (from 답답하다) is a uniquely Korean feeling word that covers a whole family of 'closed-in' sensations: physically stuffy/cramped (a tiny room, tight clothes, a congested chest when sick), AND emotionally stifled/frustrated when you can't get through — communication is blocked, a slow person won't understand, you're stuck and powerless. The unifying image is 'blocked, can't breathe, can't get out.' This feeling is crucially different from 짜증나다 ('irritated') and 화나다 ('angry'): 짜증나다 is prickly annoyance at small things; 화나다 is outward anger directed at someone; but 답답하다 is the INWARD, helpless, suffocating frustration of being stuck — often with no one clear to blame. There is no single English word for it, which is exactly why English speakers default to 화나요 ('angry') when a Korean would say 답답해요 ('stifled/stuck'). A stronger sibling idiom is 속(이) 터지다 ('my insides burst') for extreme 답답함. Register: 답답해요 polite, 답답해 반말. Mark the cause with -아서/-때문에; the stifling thing can also be the grammatical subject: 가슴이 답답해요 ('my chest feels tight').

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 답답하다 = 'to be stuffy/blocked.' The real meaning spans physical (a cramped room, a congested chest) AND emotional (blocked communication, stuck with no exit). The thread is the same blocked, can't-breathe sensation in both domains — that's what makes it uniquely Korean.

Use 답답해요 freely with close friends and family when venting about a situation — a room, a relationship, a slow process. 답답해 is 반말. With superiors or in formal situations, soften: 좀 힘드네요 or describe the problem neutrally. Never direct it at a person's face in a formal setting.

vs. 짜증나요: petty irritation at a specific thing, more outward. vs. 화나요: real anger directed at someone — more explosive. vs. 속상해요: heartsore upset about a loss or loved one's pain. 답답해요 = inward, helpless, boxed-in stifling. There is no English word — that's why English speakers misfire.
답답해 죽겠어요 (maxed-out frustration), 가슴이 답답해요 ('my chest is tight'), 속 터져요 (idiom: 'my insides are bursting'), 답답한 마음 ('a stifled/frustrated heart'). Cause takes -아서/-때문에.

(1) Defaulting to 화나요 for the stuck, can't-get-through feeling — 화나다 is anger, 답답하다 is stifled helplessness; different emotions. (2) Missing the PHYSICAL dimension — 가슴이 답답해요 is 'my chest feels tight (stuffy/congested),' not metaphorical. (3) Saying 답답나요 by analogy with 짜증나요 — it's 답답해요 (adjective), never 답답나요.

mistakes: Using 화나요 for the stuck, can't-get-through feeling.
화나다 is outward anger at someone. The helpless, boxed-in 'I can't make this work/get through' feeling is 답답해요. They're different emotions.
Forcing one English word and missing the physical sense.
답답하다 also means physically stuffy/cramped (room, chest, clothes): 가슴이 답답해요 ('my chest feels tight'). It's not only emotional.
Saying 답답나요 like 짜증나요.
답답하다 is an adjective: 답답해요, not 답답나요. Only 짜증 takes 나다. Keep 답답해요.

english: I feel a little hurt / let down (by someone close)
usage: I feel a bit hurt / let down
Polite; the quiet, wistful disappointment when someone close didn't show up for you
반말, to a close friend or family member — tender, not aggressive
네요 voices it gently and opens the door for the other person to respond
Why are you being so cold? It hurts me.
Direct but still tender; pushing back on distance without starting a fight
examples: A: 생일인 거 몰랐어요. / B: 아, 그래도 좀 서운했어요.
A: I didn't know it was your birthday. / B: Ah, still... I was a little hurt.
A/B exchange showing 서운하다 as gentle, non-aggressive hurt — the B doesn't escalate, just gently admits the sting
나만 빼고 갔다고? 좀 서운하다.
You went without me? That kind of stings.
반말 grumble of being left out — playful-wistful, not angry
벌써 가신다니 서운하네요. 더 계시지.
You're leaving already? I'm sad to see you go. Do stay longer.
서운하다 at parting — warm, regretful, not upset; -지 wishes they'd stay
nuance: 서운해요 (from 서운하다) is one of the most important feeling words in Korean relationships and has no clean English equivalent. It is the soft, wistful hurt/disappointment you feel when someone CLOSE — a friend, family member, partner — does less than you hoped: they forgot to call, left you out, didn't notice your effort, or are leaving sooner than you'd like. The feeling is gentle and tinged with affection: you say it BECAUSE you care about them, not to attack. The contrast to nail is 섭섭하다 (a near-synonym, almost interchangeable, maybe a touch more 'sad to part') versus 화나다 ('angry') and 실망하다 ('disappointed in someone's character/standards'). Say 화났어요 and you've declared a fight; say 실망했어요 and you've judged their character harshly; say 서운했어요 and you've gently shown that their distance hurt because you're close. This is the phrase that repairs relationships without breaking them. Register: 서운해요 polite, 서운해 반말. Mark the cause with -아서/-니까: 연락 안 해서 서운했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is enormous: with no equivalent word, learners reach for 상처받았어요 ('I was wounded' — too strong, implies deep damage) or 실망했어요 (too judgmental) when the warm, fixable feeling is 서운해요.

structuredNuance.t: 서운하다 has no clean literal origin for learners, but the feeling is precise: the soft, wistful sting when someone close didn't show up for you as much as you hoped. It is tinged with affection — you feel it BECAUSE you care. It is not anger, not cold disappointment, not wounded pride.

ONLY between close people — friends, family, partners. To a stranger or in formal settings it would be out of place and odd. 서운해요 is polite-intimate; 서운해 is 반말. Never use it with strangers, bosses (unless very close), or in professional complaints — those need neutral language.

vs. 섭섭하다: near-synonym, almost interchangeable; slightly more 'sad to part' in feeling. vs. 화나다: anger, signals conflict. vs. 실망하다: disappointed in someone's character/standards — harsh judgment. vs. 상처받다: 'I was wounded/damaged' — too strong for a small letdown. 서운하다 is the gentle, relational one.
서운하네요 (soft observation), 서운했어요 (past: 'I was hurt'), 서운하게 ('in a way that hurts': 서운하게 왜 그래), 많이 서운하시겠어요 ('you must be so hurt' — honorific empathy). Cause with -아서/-니까.

No English word exists, so learners misfire: 상처받았어요 ('I was wounded') is too strong for a small letdown; 실망했어요 ('I was disappointed') is too judgmental. The warm, fixable, relational hurt is 서운해요. Also don't confuse with 억울하다 ('I feel wronged/treated unjustly') — that involves perceived unfairness, not relationship closeness.

mistakes: Using 화났어요 when you mean 서운했어요.
화나다 is anger and signals conflict. 서운하다 is gentle, affectionate hurt that someone close let you down. To repair rather than fight, say 서운했어요.
Reaching for 상처받았어요 ('I was wounded').
That's too strong for a small letdown — it implies deep damage. For 'you kind of hurt my feelings,' the soft word is 서운했어요.
Translating it as cold 'disappointed' with 실망했어요.
실망하다 judges someone's character/standards harshly. 서운하다 is warm and relational ('I wish you'd cared more'). Don't swap them; the tone is opposite.

english: I feel relieved and unburdened (a weight lifted)
usage: Polite; the clean, cleared-out relief after a burden finally lifts
반말, to a close friend after something heavy is over
What a total load off my chest
속이 ('insides') + 다 ('completely') names the bodily release — very vivid
Compound of 시원하다 (refreshed) + 섭섭하다 (a little sad) — for when the relief is tinged with something to let go of
examples: A: 드디어 논문 제출했어요! / B: 진짜요? 후련하겠다!
A: I finally submitted my thesis! / B: Really? You must feel so relieved!
A/B exchange: 후련하겠다 ('you must feel unburdened') is the natural empathy response to someone finishing something big
할 말 다 하고 나니까 속이 후련해요.
After saying everything I needed to, I feel a weight off my chest.
후련함 from finally getting something off your chest; -고 나니까 = 'now that I've...'
오래 미루던 일을 끝내서 후련하면서도 좀 시원섭섭해요.
Finishing the thing I'd put off so long, I feel relieved but also a little bittersweet.
Pairs 후련하다 with 시원섭섭하다 for the nuanced bittersweet version
nuance: 후련해요 (from 후련하다) is the clean, lightened, cleared-out RELIEF you feel right after a heavy burden lifts — exams end, you finally say what was bottled up, a long worry resolves, you have a good cry. The image is your chest and insides (속) opening up and breathing freely; it is the natural opposite of 답답하다 ('stifled'). Often paired with 속이: 속이 후련해요 ('what a load off'). The word to distinguish it from is 시원하다, which overlaps a lot ('refreshing/relieving') but literally means 'cool/refreshing' and covers cold drinks, cool weather, and even a hot bath that 'hits the spot' — 후련하다 is specifically the EMOTIONAL/psychological unburdening, while 시원하다 is broader and more physical. Another nearby word is 안심하다 ('to be reassured that a worry is OK' — relief from anxiety about an outcome), vs. 후련하다's relief from a carried weight. And 다행이에요 ('thank goodness it turned out OK') comments on the situation, not the bodily feeling. The bittersweet cousin 시원섭섭하다 (relieved but sad to let go) is essential for endings. Register: 후련해요 polite, 후련해 반말. Mark the cause with -아서/-고 나니까.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 후련하다 = 'to be clear/unburdened.' The real meaning is a PHYSICAL sensation of your chest/insides opening up after a weight lifts — not just a mental 'that's good news.' This bodily unburdening is what distinguishes it from 다행이에요 or 안심하다.

Use after finishing something long and heavy: exams, a hard project, a difficult conversation, a cry. 후련해요 is polite-casual; 후련해 is 반말. Fine with anyone — friends, family, coworkers. The vivid 속이 다 후련해요 is warmly colloquial; for huge, long-pent relief, 십 년 묵은 체증이 내려간 것 같아요 is the vivid idiom.

vs. 다행이에요: comments on a situation turning out OK ('thank goodness'). vs. 안심하다: relief that a specific worry is resolved ('I'm reassured'). vs. 시원하다: broadly cool/refreshing (physical). 후련하다 = the felt bodily unburdening of a carried weight. These are not interchangeable.
속이 다 후련하다 (full release), 후련했어요 (past), 후련하겠다 ('you must feel relieved' — empathy), 시원섭섭하다 (bittersweet relief). Idiom for huge relief: 십 년 묵은 체증이 내려간 것 같아요 ('like a ten-year knot finally untied').

The pitfall is using 다행이에요 ('thank goodness') for this bodily unburdening — they're different kinds of relief: 다행이에요 = 'the situation turned out OK,' 후련하다 = 'I physically feel the weight gone.' Also don't swap in 시원해요 for emotional relief — 시원하다 is broader and physical.

mistakes: Using 다행이에요 for the unburdened feeling.
다행이에요 = 'thank goodness it turned out OK' (a comment on the situation). The felt 'weight lifted off my chest' is 후련해요. Different relief.
Defaulting to 시원해요 for emotional relief.
시원하다 is broad 'cool/refreshing' (drinks, weather, soup). For the specifically emotional unburdening, 후련해요 is sharper and more correct.
Confusing it with 안심해요.
안심하다 = relief from worry/anxiety ('I'm reassured it's fine'). 후련하다 = relief from a weight/burden lifting. Match the source of relief.

usage: Half-to-yourself mutter; warm envy that escapes as an exhaled exclamation
아 ('ahh') vents the wistful envy even more — very natural spoken Korean
Polite -네요 said aloud to the person; shares the observation gently
Playful set phrase to tease yourself or lighten jealousy in a group
examples: A: 나 이번에 유럽 여행 갔다 왔어! / B: 와… 부럽다 진짜. 나도 가고 싶다.
A: I just got back from a trip to Europe! / B: Wow… I'm seriously jealous. I want to go too.
A/B exchange showing the most natural conversational mutter; the warmth comes from the shared wish (-고 싶다)
둘이 사이좋은 거 보면 부럽네요.
Seeing how close you two are makes me envious.
Polite 부럽네요 said directly to the person — a soft compliment on their relationship
나도 그런 거 갖고 싶다. 부럽다 진짜.
I want one of those too. Man, I'm jealous.
Pairing with -고 싶다 ('I want...') to make the wishful side explicit
nuance: 부럽다 진짜 is the spoken, exclamatory form of 부럽다 ('to be envious') — Koreans constantly drop the polite ending and just exhale 부럽다 (often with 진짜 'for real' or 아 'ahh') as a warm, wistful 'lucky you / I wish that were me.' It is the SAME friendly envy as 부러워요 but in its most natural muttered shape. You can say the bare 부럽다 even around elders without it being rude, because the exclamatory adjective-다 form functions like thinking out loud rather than 반말 directed AT someone. To say it politely straight to the person, use 부럽네요 ('I must say, I envy you'). The contrast to keep in mind is the dark 질투(나다) ('possessive jealousy') — 부럽다 is never hostile. There's also the famous playful phrase 부러우면 지는 거다 ('if you're envious, you've already lost') used to tease yourself for being jealous. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, learners over-formalize and only ever use 부러워요, so they miss the much more natural spoken 부럽다 and sound stiff; second, they confuse the plain-form exclamation 부럽다 (fine to mutter even around elders) with using full 반말 verbs or commands at an elder (not fine). Also mark what you envy with 이/가 if you name it: 네가 부럽다, not 너를 부럽다.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: '나는 부럽다' = 'I am envious.' The real meaning: a warm, involuntary exhale of friendly envy — 'lucky you, I wish that were me.' Absolutely not hostile or bitter; it functions like a compliment.

부럽다 진짜 is 반말/informal and is used freely among close peers. As a bare exclamation (without 진짜), 부럽다 can also be muttered around elders without being rude — because exclamatory adjective-다 is like thinking aloud. To address someone politely, use 부럽네요. Never appropriate in formal written or professional communication.

vs. 부러워요: the textbook polite form — grammatically complete but in fast speech sounds a touch formal. vs. 질투나요: dark, possessive jealousy — completely wrong register for friendly envy. vs. 부럽네요: polite observation form, gentle enough to say to the person directly. 부럽다 진짜 is the most natural spoken mutter.
아 진짜 부럽다, 완전 부럽다, 부럽네요 (polite version), 부러우면 지는 거예요 (joke). To name the envied thing: 네가 부럽다 / 그게 부럽다 (이/가, never 을/를).

Two traps: (1) only using formal 부러워요 and sounding stiff — Koreans in real speech constantly say 부럽다; (2) thinking 부럽다 is rude to elders — exclamatory adjective-다 is like thinking aloud, which is acceptable even near seniors. Mark the envied thing with 이/가, not 을/를.

mistakes: Thinking the bare 부럽다 is rude to elders.
Exclamatory adjective-다 is like thinking aloud, not 반말 aimed at someone. Muttering 부럽다 near an elder is fine; to address them say 부럽네요.
Always saying 부러워요 and never the natural 부럽다.
Koreans constantly exclaim 부럽다 / 부럽다 진짜. Only using the textbook 부러워요 sounds stiff. Learn the muttered form too.
Adding 을/를 to what you envy.
It's 네가 부럽다 / 그게 부럽다 with 이/가, not 너를 부럽다. The envied thing/situation takes the subject marker.

hangul: 짜증 좀 안 나게 해 주세요
english: Please don't make this so frustrating / annoying
usage: 짜증 좀 안 나게 해 주세요
Please don't make this so annoying
Polite-ish but pointed; use only when genuinely fed up — not casual small talk
반말, to a close friend who's intentionally winding you up
You're really getting on my nerves
사람 ('a person') stands for 'me'; a muttered aside — sharp even among friends
Cleaner, less crude way to ask someone to stop — safer in most situations
examples: A: 자꾸 끼어들지 마세요. / B: 미안해요. / A: 짜증 나게 하지 말아요, 진짜.
A: Stop cutting in, please. / B: Sorry. / A: Don't make this annoying, seriously.
A/B exchange showing how this escalates — the second line only lands after a first warning
아, 진짜 사람 짜증 나게 하네.
Ugh, you're really getting on my nerves.
Muttered 사람 짜증 나게 하다 about someone exasperating — blunt and clearly about them
일부러 그러는 거예요? 짜증 나게.
Are you doing it on purpose? So annoying.
Trailing 짜증 나게 as a sharp aside — the accusation that it might be deliberate makes it sting more
nuance: This entry teaches the CAUSATIVE pattern — 짜증 나게 하다 ('to make someone annoyed/irritated'), built from 짜증(이) 나다 plus -게 하다 ('make it so that...'). It's how you point at the SOURCE of irritation instead of just venting your own state. Be warned: it's confrontational. 짜증 나게 하지 마(세요) ('stop annoying me') and 사람 짜증 나게 하네 ('you're getting on my nerves') are reserved for people you're close to or when you're genuinely fed up — never to staff, seniors, or in polite company, where you'd say 좀 그만해 주세요 ('please stop') or describe the problem calmly. The milder alternative is 신경 쓰이다 / 신경 쓰게 하다 ('to bother / weigh on the mind'), which carries more distraction/worry and less open 'you're pissing me off.' The English-speaker grammar pitfall is structural: learners try 너 나를 짜증해 (wrong on two counts) — 짜증(이) 나다 is intransitive, and to cause someone to feel it you need the causative -게 하다: 짜증 나게 하다. So 'you're annoying me' is 너 (나를) 짜증 나게 해, NOT 너 짜증나. Note: 사람 here is not a specific person — idiomatically 사람 짜증 나게 하다 means 'you're irritating me.' Default to softer phrasing unless you truly mean to push back hard.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 짜증 나게 하다 = 'to make (something/someone) cause irritation to arise.' The real meaning: 'you are the SOURCE of my annoyance, stop it.' This is not a neutral observation — it is a direct confrontation, pointing the finger at a person's behavior.

Only appropriate with close friends/family when genuinely fed up. Do NOT use with staff, seniors, strangers, coworkers above you, or in any formal setting — it will cause a conflict or seem rude/childish. Use 좀 그만해 주세요 or neutrally describe the issue in all other contexts.

vs. 신경 쓰게 하다: milder 'you're on my mind / distracting me' — more worried than annoyed. vs. 귀찮게 하다: 'to bother/hassle me (laziness frame)' — different annoyance type. vs. 화나게 하다: 'to make me angry' — even stronger, implies real anger. 짜증 나게 하다 is in the irritation register, not full anger.
짜증 나게 하지 마 (반말 prohibition), 사람 짜증 나게 하네 (muttered blunt complaint), 짜증 나게 왜 그래 ('why are you being so annoying?'), 좀 그만해 주세요 (polite neutral alternative).

(1) Saying 너 짜증나 to mean 'you're annoying me' — that actually means 'YOU feel irritated.' To say someone annoys YOU, use the causative: 너 (나를) 짜증 나게 해. (2) Structural error: 짜증(이) 나다 is intransitive; 나를 짜증해 is doubly wrong (wrong verb + no such word). The causative -게 하다 is essential.

mistakes: Saying 너 짜증나 to mean 'you're annoying me'.
너 짜증나 means 'YOU feel annoyed.' To say someone annoys YOU, use the causative: 너 (나를) 짜증 나게 해. Direction matters.
Using it with staff or seniors.
짜증 나게 하다 is blunt and confrontational. With staff/seniors say 좀 그만해 주세요 or calmly state the issue. Reserve this for close, genuinely-fed-up moments.
Writing 짜증나게해 as one chunk wrongly.
It's 짜증(이) 나다 + -게 하다 → 짜증 나게 하다. Spacing/structure: the 나다 + 게 하다 causative is what carries 'make someone annoyed.'

usage: Polite; explicitly names the heart as grammatical subject — the most natural full form
두근거리다 ('to pound/throb') for the physical heartbeat — stronger and can be excitement OR fear
Set phrase for cards, messages, and warm sign-offs: 'with an eager heart, I...'
The nervous-jitters cousin — for contrast; can be bad nerves, not sweet anticipation
examples: A: 그 사람 좋아해요? / B: 응, 그 사람만 보면 마음이 설레.
A: Do you like them? / B: Yeah, my heart flutters every time I just see them.
A/B exchange: -만 보면 = 'every time I just see...' — the most natural romantic flutter sentence
내일 콘서트라 벌써 가슴이 두근거리고 마음이 설레요.
The concert's tomorrow, so my heart's already pounding and fluttering.
Pairing 두근거리다 (pounding) with 설레다 (fluttering) to show the compound excitement
설레는 마음으로 답장 기다릴게요.
I'll wait for your reply with an eager heart.
설레는 마음으로 as a warm, slightly literary sign-off in a message or letter
nuance: 마음이 설레요 makes explicit what 설레다 implies — that it's the HEART (마음, the heart/mind) that flutters. This teaches the natural Korean subject pattern: body/heart words often take 이/가 as the grammatical subject of feeling verbs (마음이 설레요, 가슴이 두근거려요, 가슴이 답답해요), which is structurally very different from English 'I feel...' Mastering this pattern fixes a whole class of grammatical errors. The flutter words to keep straight: 설레다 = sweet, welcome anticipatory flutter; 두근거리다 / 두근두근하다 = the heart physically POUNDING (can be excitement OR fear/nerves); 떨리다 = trembling/nervous jitters (often bad nerves). For a happy crush, 마음이 설레요 and 가슴이 두근거려요 overlap beautifully; but if you only say 두근거려요 it's ambiguous (could be fear), while 설레요 specifies the happy kind. The lovely set phrase 설레는 마음으로 ('with an eager/fluttering heart') is standard in warm messages and cards. Register: 설레요 polite. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: (1) saying 나는 설레요 and forgetting that Korean prefers 마음이/가슴이 as the subject for heart-feelings; (2) the perennial misspelling 설레여요/설래요 — always 설레요 / 설렜어요.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: '마음(heart/mind) + 이(subject) + 설레요(flutters)' = 'the heart flutters.' This is NOT a metaphor in Korean — the heart literally flutters as the grammatical subject. Mastering this body-as-subject structure (마음이, 가슴이, 마음이) is a key step beyond intermediate Korean.

Use freely in any warm context — romance, travel excitement, a first snow, a concert. 마음이 설레요 is polite; 마음이 설레 is 반말. The set phrase 설레는 마음으로 is slightly literary and fits cards or messages. With close friends, 설레 alone is the natural short form.

vs. 두근거리다: physical heart pounding — can be excitement or fear, ambiguous. 설레다 always means the happy flutter. vs. 떨리다: nervous trembling, often bad nerves. vs. 기대돼요: 'I'm looking forward to it' — mental anticipation, cooler and less physical. 마음이 설레요 = heart physically flutters with sweet anticipation.
마음이 설레요 (full polite), 설레 (반말 short), 설렜어요 (past: 'my heart was fluttering'), 설레는 마음으로 (set phrase for messages), 두근두근해요 (onomatopoeia pounding form).

(1) Saying 나는 설레요 and missing that Korean puts 마음이/가슴이 as subject for heart-feelings — learn the body-subject pattern. (2) Misspelling: 설레여요 and 설래요 are very common errors; the stem is 설레-, so it's always 설레요 / 설렜어요. Lock these in.

mistakes: Saying 나는 설레요 and skipping the heart subject.
Korean heart-feelings often take 마음이/가슴이 as subject: 마음이 설레요. It's a different structure from English 'I feel...'. Learn the body-as-subject pattern.
Using 두근거려요 assuming it's always happy.
두근거리다 is the heart POUNDING — could be excitement or fear. For specifically sweet anticipation, 설레요 makes the happy meaning clear.
Misspelling as 설래요 / 설레여요.
Stem is 설레-: present 설레요, past 설렜어요. 설래요 and 설레여요 are common errors. Lock in 설레요.

usage: Polite; 왠지 ('for some reason I can't pin down') + soft -네요 of shared realization
반말, to a friend — the most natural casual spoken form
뭔가 ('somehow/something') variant — slightly vaguer, still warm
I'm giddy for no good reason (and I know it)
괜히 ('for no good reason, pointlessly') — self-aware flutter, slightly self-deprecating
examples: 첫눈이 와서 그런가, 왠지 설레네요.
Maybe because the first snow fell — somehow I feel giddy.
왠지 + 네요 musing about a vague happy flutter; -어서 그런가 = 'maybe because...'
A: 오늘 왠지 설레지 않아요? / B: 맞아요, 저도 그래요.
A: Don't you feel giddy today, somehow? / B: Right, me too.
A/B exchange using -지 않아요? to invite agreement — perfect for the shared atmospheric flutter
내일부터 새 직장이라 괜히 설레요.
I start a new job tomorrow, so I'm giddy for no real reason.
괜히 admits the flutter is hard to logically justify — self-aware and charming
nuance: 왠지 설레네요 layers two very natural Korean pieces onto 설레다: 왠지 ('somehow, for some reason I can't name') and the soft sentence-ending -네요 (mild realization/observation, inviting the listener to share the feeling). The result is the cozy, atmospheric 'ooh, somehow this gives me butterflies' you say about first snow, a song, a season changing, a small good omen — not romance specifically. Mastering 왠지 / 괜히 / 뭔가 here is the real lesson: they're vibe-softeners Koreans sprinkle constantly: 왠지 ('for some reason'), 괜히 ('for no good reason/pointlessly,' often self-deprecating), 뭔가 ('something/somehow'). And -네요 vs. -요: 설레요 states the flutter flatly; 설레네요 adds 'oh, I notice I'm fluttering' and invites the listener into it — warmer and more conversational. Register: 설레네요 polite; 설레 반말; 설레네 is 반말 informal. The English-speaker pitfall is primarily spelling: 왠지 ('somehow,' from 왜인지 = 'why-ever') is constantly confused with and miswritten as 웬지 — remember only 왠지 is correct for 'somehow'; 웬 belongs to 웬일/웬만하면. Also: don't translate 왠지 as a literal 'why' — it's an atmospheric 'vibe' word, not a question.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 왠지 = 'for some reason' (from 왜인지 'why-ever'), 설레다 = 'flutters,' -네요 = observational ending. The real meaning: a soft, cozy, atmospheric observation of a feeling you can't fully explain — 'somehow I have butterflies and I'm sharing that with you.'

Use in warm, casual conversation about seasonal moments, music, new starts, gentle excitement — not romantic confessions (for that 마음이 설레요 is more direct). 왠지 설레네요 is polite-conversational; 왠지 설레 is 반말. The -네요 ending makes it feel like shared musing rather than a declaration.

왠지 = 'for some reason' (can't name why). 괜히 = 'for no good reason, pointlessly' (often with a self-deprecating awareness). 뭔가 = 'somehow / something' (the vaguest). All soften 설레요 but with different shades. 설레요 alone is a clear declaration; 왠지/괜히/뭔가 + 설레요 admits the feeling is a bit mysterious or unwarranted.
왠지 설레 (반말), 괜히 설레요 (self-aware flutter), 뭔가 설레요 (vaguer), 왠지 설레서 잠이 안 와요 ('I'm too giddy to sleep, somehow'). Polite: 설레네요; 반말: 설레; formal: avoid — instead say 기대가 됩니다.

(1) Spelling trap: 왠지 is correct ('somehow' = 왜인지); 웬지 is wrong. 웬 belongs to 웬일/웬만하면. (2) Don't translate 왠지 as a literal 'why' — it's a vibe softener, not a question. (3) Dropping 요 from 설레네: -네 alone is 반말; polite is -네요. The -네요 ending also adds warmth by inviting shared feeling.

mistakes: Writing 웬지 instead of 왠지.
'Somehow' is 왠지 (from 왜인지). 웬지 is wrong; 웬 belongs to 웬일/웬만하면. For the giddy-for-some-reason feeling: 왠지 설레네요.
Translating 왠지 as literal 'why'.
왠지 is a vibe word meaning 'somehow/for some reason I can't pin down,' not a question 'why.' It softens the statement and makes it atmospheric, it doesn't ask anything.
Dropping 요 from 설레네 with non-intimates.
-네 alone is 반말. Politely it's 설레네요. The -네요 adds 'oh, I notice...' warmth while staying polite.

english: I'm upset / it breaks my heart (a little)
usage: Polite; heartsore distress over something that went wrong or someone who's hurting
반말, to a close friend or family when venting heartsore feelings
-아 죽겠어요 maxes the heartache — usually comic unless the situation is truly serious
Honorific empathy form — how you comfort someone with this word
examples: 아끼던 컵이 깨져서 속상해요.
My favorite cup broke, so I'm upset.
속상하다 for a small personal loss; 아끼던 = 'that I had treasured'
A: 시험 망쳤어요. / B: 많이 속상하겠다. 이번 한 번이야, 다음에 잘하면 돼.
A: I bombed the exam. / B: You must be so upset. It's just this once — you'll do well next time.
A/B exchange: 속상하겠다 as natural empathy; B comforts with 이번 한 번이야
애가 아픈데 해 줄 게 없어서 너무 속상해요.
My child is sick and there's nothing I can do — it breaks my heart.
속상하다 for the helpless, tender heartache of a loved one's pain — not anger, just love-pain
nuance: 속상해요 (from 속상하다, literally 속 'insides' + 상하다 'to be spoiled/hurt') is the heartsore, distressed UPSET you feel when something goes wrong and it pains your insides — a treasured object breaks, your child is hurting, your effort failed, someone you love is in trouble. It is warmer and more tender than anger: the 'aw, this makes my heart sink' feeling, often with a note of helplessness. It is important to distinguish from neighbors: 화나요 ('angry') is outward and aimed at a person; 짜증나요 ('annoyed') is petty irritation; 서운해요 ('hurt/let down') is specifically about someone close disappointing you; but 속상하다 is broad heart-pain over a bad situation or loss, not necessarily anyone's fault. It is also gentler than 슬프다 ('sad,' bigger grief). A huge use of the word is COMFORTING others: 많이 속상하시겠어요 ('you must be so upset') is how you show genuine empathy. Register: 속상해요 polite, 속상해 반말. Mark the cause with -아서/-니까: 깨져서 속상해요. The English-speaker pitfall is defaulting to 화나요 for every 'upset' — English 'upset' covers both angry and heartsore, but Korean separates them: heartsore distress is 속상해요.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 속 ('insides/gut') + 상하다 ('to be spoiled/hurt') = 'my insides are hurt.' The real meaning: tender, heartsore distress — not rage, not grief, but the pained 'my heart sinks' feeling when something dear goes wrong or someone you love is hurting.

Use with close friends and family, or in contexts where tender emotion is appropriate (children's failures, small losses, a loved one's pain). 속상해요 is polite; 속상해 is 반말. The comforting honorific 많이 속상하시겠어요 is essential for empathy. Don't use it in formal professional complaints — describe the issue neutrally instead.

vs. 화나요: outward anger aimed at a person — different emotion entirely. vs. 짜증나요: petty prickly irritation at a small thing. vs. 서운해요: hurt/letdown specifically by someone close. vs. 슬퍼요: sad (bigger, more general grief). 속상해요 = tender, heartache distress over something going wrong, often no one's fault.
속상해 죽겠어요 (max, comic), 많이 속상하시겠어요 (honorific empathy), 속상했어요 (past), 속상하겠다 ('you must be upset' — empathy form). Cause takes -아서/-니까: 깨져서 속상해요.

English 'upset' covers both angry and heartsore — Korean separates them. 화나요 = angry (directed at a person); 속상해요 = heartsore/distressed (about a situation). Defaulting to 화나요 for every 'upset' sends the wrong message. Also don't confuse with 배탈 ('upset stomach') — emotional upset is 속상하다, stomach trouble is 배탈이 나다.

mistakes: Translating 'upset' as 화나요.
English 'upset' is usually heartsore distress = 속상해요, not anger. 화나요 means you're mad at someone, which changes the message. Default to 속상해요.
Using 속상해요 for an upset STOMACH.
Emotional upset is 속상하다. A bad stomach is 배탈(이) 나다 / 속이 안 좋다. Don't say 속상해요 when you mean indigestion.
Attaching an object: 그 일을 속상해요.
속상하다 describes your state. Mark the cause: 그 일 때문에 속상해요 ('I'm upset because of that').

english: It's so vexing / I'm green with envy-and-frustration
usage: It's so vexing / it gets my goat
Polite-casual; the taunted, can't-have-it frustration with an edge of sour-grapes envy
반말, to a friend — playful or genuinely exasperated depending on tone
약(을) 올리다 = to taunt; the causative — you'll hear this one even more than 약 올라
Idiom: '배(stomach) 아프다(hurts)' = resentful envy of others' luck — from the famous proverb
examples: A: 나만 안 됐다고? / B: 그건 진짜 약 올리네.
A: Only I didn't get it? / B: That's genuinely vexing.
A/B exchange: 약 올리네 ('that vexes me') — B uses the causative form, pointing at the situation as the source
동생이 자꾸 자랑해서 약 올라요.
My sibling keeps bragging, so it's getting on my nerves.
약 오르다 from someone flaunting — the annoyed-envious mix
그만 약 올려요! 나도 갖고 싶단 말이에요.
Stop taunting me! I want one too, you know.
Causative 약 올리다 + -단 말이에요 ('I'm telling you/I mean it') for comic frustration
nuance: 약 올라요 (from 약(이) 오르다, literally 'the 약/sap rises') is a vivid colloquial feeling: the prickly, vexed, 'argh, why not me / stop rubbing it in' frustration — a blend of envy and being deliberately teased or provoked. You feel 약 오르다 when others have what you can't, when someone flaunts or taunts you, when you're SO close but just miss out. The intensity is playful-to-genuinely-annoyed depending on tone, and this expression is very common among friends and siblings. The crucial paired phrase is the CAUSATIVE 약(을) 올리다 ('to taunt, to rub it in, to get a rise out of someone'): 약 올리지 마 ('don't tease me') is everyday speech and you need to distinguish which direction you're using. Distinguish from plain 부럽다 (warm, clean envy with no bite) and 짜증나다 (general irritation without the envious taunted edge): 약 오르다 specifically carries that sour-grapes, taunted frustration. A related idiom is 배(가) 아프다 ('my stomach hurts' = I'm resentfully envious), from the proverb 사촌이 땅을 사면 배가 아프다 ('when your cousin buys land, your stomach aches'). Register: casual/colloquial — friends only. The pitfall: (1) mixing 약 오르다 (I feel vexed) with 약 올리다 (to taunt someone); (2) reading 약 as 'medicine' (it's idiomatic sap/bile here); (3) using it in formal settings where 부럽다 is more appropriate.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 약(sap/bile) + 오르다(rise) = 'the sap rises in me.' The real meaning: the prickly, sour-grapes vexation of being taunted, missing out, or watching someone flaunt what you can't have. Not just envy (부럽다) and not just irritation (짜증) — it has a specifically goaded, provoked quality.

Strictly casual/colloquial — close friends, family, siblings. In formal settings it sounds immature or rude; use 부럽다 or describe the situation neutrally. 약 올라요 is polite-casual; 약 올라 is 반말. Very common in sibling banter, friend teasing, and sports commentary.

vs. 부럽다: clean, warm, friendly envy with no hostile edge. 약 오르다 has the taunted/provoked element — someone is rubbing it in. vs. 짜증나다: general prickly irritation; 약 오르다 specifically involves envy and being goaded. vs. 배(가) 아프다: resentful envy of someone's good luck/success (proverb-based idiom, a bit stronger).
약 올라 (반말), 약 올라요 (polite-casual), 약 올리지 마 (prohibition: causative), 약 올리다 (causative verb: 'to taunt'). Related idiom: 배가 아파요 ('I'm enviously sour'). Cause takes 때문에: 자기 자랑 때문에 약 올라.

(1) Confusing 약 오르다 ('I feel vexed') with 약 올리다 ('to taunt/vex someone else') — the voice reverses who is feeling what. (2) Reading 약 as 'medicine' — here it is idiomatic sap/bile, not 약 'medicine.' (3) Overusing in polite/formal settings — reserve for genuinely casual moments.

mistakes: Confusing 약 오르다 (feel vexed) with 약 올리다 (taunt).
약 올라요 = 'I feel vexed/taunted.' To tell someone to stop teasing: 약 올리지 마(세요). Mixing the two reverses who's doing what.
Reading 약 as 'medicine'.
Here 약 is idiomatic (the rising sap/bile), not 약 'medicine.' 약 올라요 means 'I'm vexed,' nothing to do with drugs.
Using 약 올라요 in formal/polite settings.
It's colloquial and a bit slangy. With seniors or in formal talk, use 부럽다 or neutrally describe the situation. Save 약 올라 for friends.

english: Don't be so cold/distant — it hurts me
usage: Don't be so distant, it hurts
Polite-intimate; gently protests a close person's coldness without starting a fight
Why are you being so cold?
반말, to a close friend/family — tender reproach, not an accusation
섭섭하다 near-synonym version; equally common and interchangeable in this phrase
Saying it that way hurts, you know
-죠 appeals for shared understanding — softer than a direct complaint
examples: A: 왜 이렇게 차가워요. / B: 차가운 게 아니에요. / A: 서운하게 그러지 마세요, 진짜로.
A: Why are you so cold? / B: I'm not being cold. / A: Don't act in a hurtful way, really.
Three-line exchange showing the phrase in a real relational push-back — A tries gentle confrontation without escalating
가족끼린데 서운하게 왜 그래.
We're family — why are you being so cold?
끼리 ('among ourselves') appeals to closeness; gentle reproach using 반말
밥도 안 먹고 가면 제가 서운하죠. 조금만 더 있다 가세요.
If you leave without even eating, of course I'm hurt. Stay a little longer.
Warm 서운하죠 to make someone stay — -죠 signals 'you know this would hurt me'
nuance: This entry teaches how to TELL someone they're hurting you — the relational repair move built on 서운하다. 서운하게 그러지 마세요 (lit. 'don't act in a way that makes me 서운') is how Koreans gently push back when someone close is being cold, distant, or neglectful — WITHOUT escalating to a fight. The tone is intimate and a little vulnerable; you're saying 'you're hurting me because I care about you.' This only works with people you're close to (family, close friends, a partner); to a stranger or in formal settings it would be out of place. The near-synonym 섭섭하다 is fully interchangeable here (섭섭하게 왜 그러세요). Crucially, contrast this with the angry/blaming alternatives: 왜 이렇게 차갑게 굴어요? leans colder/accusatory, and 화내지 마 assumes anger — but 서운하게 그러지 마 keeps it tender and reparative. The grammar lesson is the adverbial -게 + 그러다 pattern: 서운하게 그러다 = 'to act in a 서운-causing way,' a super common Korean construction (속상하게 하지 마, 섭섭하게 하지 마). The English-speaker pitfall is (1) not having this move at all — English speakers either bottle it up or escalate to 'I'm angry,' missing the gentle 서운 repair; (2) confusing 그러다 ('to act/do so') with 그렇다 ('to be so') — only 그러지 마 is correct; (3) misjudging the register — this is always intimate, never formal.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: '서운하게(in a hurtful way) + 그러지(don't act) + 마세요(please)' = 'please don't act in a way that causes me 서운-feeling.' The real meaning: 'your coldness is hurting me — I'm telling you gently because I care, not to attack you.' A repair phrase, not an escalation.

ONLY with close people — family, close friends, partners. Never to a stranger, boss, or in professional settings — it is too intimate and vulnerable. 서운하게 그러지 마세요 is polite-intimate; 서운하게 왜 그래 is 반말. The relationship closeness is required for it to land correctly. To a stranger it sounds presumptuous.

vs. 섭섭하게 왜 그러세요: near-synonym, almost interchangeable. vs. 차갑게 굴지 마세요: 'don't be cold' — more accusatory, less vulnerable. vs. 화내지 마: 'don't be angry' — assumes anger, misframes the feeling. 서운하게 그러지 마세요 is the uniquely tender, relational repair phrase.
서운하게 왜 그래 (반말), 섭섭하게 하지 마세요 (near-synonym form), 그렇게 말하면 서운하죠 ('-죠 appeal'), 서운하게 했어요? ('Did I hurt you?' — asking if you caused it).

(1) English speakers either bottle this feeling up or escalate to anger — the gentle repair move 서운하게 그러지 마 doesn't have an English equivalent, so learners miss it entirely. (2) Grammar: 그러지 마 (don't act so) uses 그러다 — don't confuse with 그렇지 마, which is unnatural. (3) Register: always intimate, never professional — using it with a stranger or boss sounds presumptuous and strange.

mistakes: Escalating to 화내지 마 / 왜 화났어 instead.
Those assume anger and can start a fight. 서운하게 그러지 마 keeps it tender — 'you're hurting me because I care' — which repairs rather than escalates.
Using it with strangers or in formal settings.
This is an intimate, vulnerable move for close relationships only. To a stranger/senior it's out of place; you'd state concerns neutrally instead.
Confusing 그러지 마 (don't act so) with 그렇지 마.
그러다 = 'to act/do so' → 그러지 마(세요) ('don't be like that'). 그렇다 = 'to be so' and doesn't take 마. Keep 서운하게 그러지 마세요.

english: Now I finally feel some relief
usage: Polite; 이제야 ('only now, at long last') + reflective -네요 = 'phew, at last'
반말, to a friend — shared exhale of relief
What a total load off my chest
속이 ('insides') + 다 ('completely') for maximum bodily release
십 년 묵은 체증이 내려간 것 같아요
Like a ten-year-old knot finally untied
The vivid idiom for huge, long-awaited relief — 'a ten-year case of indigestion finally clears'
examples: 다 말하고 나니까 이제야 좀 후련하네요.
Now that I've said it all, I finally feel some relief.
이제야 + -고 나니까 ('now that I've...') marks long-delayed release perfectly
A: 그 사람이 사과했어요? / B: 네, 그래서 이제야 속이 후련해요.
A: Did they apologize? / B: Yes, so I finally feel a weight off my chest.
A/B exchange: B's relief comes not from a task ending but from a relationship resolution — 이제야 marks how long it took
몇 년을 끌던 일이 끝나서, 십 년 묵은 체증이 내려간 것 같아요.
The thing that dragged on for years is over — like a ten-year knot finally untied.
The vivid 묵은 체증 idiom for release after years of carrying something
nuance: 이제야 좀 후련하네요 layers the time-nuance 이제야 ('only now, finally, at long last — and it took too long') and reflective -네요 onto 후련하다, producing the satisfying 'phew, AT LAST a weight is off me' you say when something you'd carried for a long time finally resolves. The real lessons here are (1) 이제야 vs. 이제: 이제 just means 'now,' but 이제야 adds 'only now / not until now,' implying it took longer than it should have — a small word that carries real felt weight; and (2) the scaling of relief idioms in Korean. For big, long-awaited release Koreans use vivid expressions: 속이 다 후련하다 ('my insides are completely cleared'), 십 년 묵은 체증이 내려가다 (lit. 'a ten-year-old case of indigestion finally clears' = enormous pent-up relief), and 한(이) 풀리다 ('a deep grudge/regret finally unravels'). Contrast 후련하다 with 시원하다 (broader, more physical 'cool/refreshing') and 다행이에요 ('thank goodness the situation turned out OK' — a comment on the situation, not a felt bodily release). Register: 후련하네요 polite; the -네요 makes it sound like genuine, just-felt realization rather than a flat report. The English-speaker pitfall: (1) using flat 이제 and missing the 'finally/at last' weight that 이제야 adds; (2) defaulting to 다행이에요 for this bodily unburdening; (3) confusing the -야 in 이제야 ('only then/at last') with the vocative 야 ('hey, you').

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 이제야(only now) + 좀(a bit) + 후련하네요(I feel relieved, I notice). The real meaning: 'FINALLY — after too long — a weight is off me.' The 이제야 is crucial: it marks that the relief was delayed, making the unburdening feel even more satisfying.

Use after something long-pent finally resolves: a long project ends, an apology finally comes, a tension breaks. 후련하네요 is polite-casual; 후련해 is 반말. The -네요 ending makes it sound like a genuine, just-felt exhale rather than a flat statement — it invites the listener to share the relief. Fine with friends, family, and casual coworkers.

vs. 다행이에요: 'thank goodness it turned out OK' — comments on the situation. vs. 안심이에요: relief that a specific worry resolved ('I'm reassured'). vs. 시원하다: broad physical 'cool/refreshing.' 이제야 후련하네요 = the BODILY unburdening of a long-carried weight, finally released. Scale up: 속이 다 후련하다 → 십 년 묵은 체증이 내려가다 for larger relief.
이제야 좀 후련해 (반말), 속이 다 후련하네요 (max bodily release), 이제야 후련하겠다 ('you must finally feel relieved' — empathy), 한이 풀렸어요 ('a deep grudge/regret is resolved'). Idiom: 십 년 묵은 체증이 내려간 것 같아요.
chips: 십 년 묵은 체증이 내려간 것 같아요

structuredNuance.t: (1) Using 이제 ('now') instead of 이제야 ('only now / at long last') — 이제야 carries the 'it took too long' weight that makes the relief feel earned. (2) Using 다행이에요 for the bodily 'weight lifted' feeling — 다행 is about a situation turning out OK, not about felt physical unburdening. (3) Confusing -야 in 이제야 (the 'only then' particle, attaches to time words) with vocative 야 ('hey').

mistakes: Using 이제 instead of 이제야 for 'finally'.
이제 = 'now'; 이제야 = 'only now / at long last,' carrying the 'it took too long' feeling. For the 'finally!' relief, use 이제야.
Substituting 다행이에요 for the 'load off my chest' feeling.
다행이에요 = 'thank goodness it turned out OK' (about the situation). The felt bodily unburdening is 후련하네요. Different kinds of relief.
Reading the -야 in 이제야 as 'hey'.
Here -야 attaches to a time word meaning 'only then/at last' (이제야 = 'only now'). It's not the vocative 야 ('hey, you'). Don't mix them up.

english: It's on my mind / it keeps bothering me
usage: It keeps bothering me / I can't stop thinking about it
Polite; something nags at your mind without your choosing — passive, mid-strength
반말, to a friend when sharing what's been on your mind
Don't worry about it / never mind it
Telling someone to let it go — extremely common kindness phrase
자꾸 ('repeatedly') + -네요 for a recurring nag you notice and share
examples: 아까 그 말이 계속 신경 쓰여요.
What you said earlier keeps bothering me.
Something said that you can't stop turning over; 계속 = 'keep/continuously'
A: 걱정돼요? / B: 걱정은 아닌데, 그냥 신경 쓰여요.
A: Are you worried? / B: Not worried exactly, but it's just on my mind.
A/B exchange distinguishing 걱정 (worry) from the milder 신경 쓰이다 (nagging/distracting) — a crucial real-world difference
그건 제가 알아서 할게요. 신경 쓰지 마세요.
I'll handle that myself. Don't worry about it.
신경 쓰지 마세요 to release someone from concern — very common and kind in Korean
nuance: 신경 쓰여요 (from 신경(이) 쓰이다, lit. '나의 nerves get used/spent on it') is the everyday word for something that NAGS at your mind passively — you can't stop thinking about a comment, a staring stranger distracts you, a small unresolved thing keeps pulling at your attention. It is mid-strength: more than nothing, less than full-blown 걱정 ('worry'). The crucial pair to master is the active vs. passive: 신경(을) 쓰다 = 'to actively pay attention to / care about / invest effort in something' (제가 신경 쓸게요 = 'I'll take care of it / I'll pay attention'), while 신경(이) 쓰이다 = the passive 'it bothers/preoccupies me without my choosing.' Learners constantly mix these: 신경 써요 means 'I actively attend to it,' while 신경 쓰여요 means 'it nags at me involuntarily.' The other essential phrase is 신경 쓰지 마(세요) ('don't bother/worry about it'), a constant kindness. Distinguish from 걱정되다 ('I'm worried,' future-oriented anxiety about an outcome) and 거슬리다 ('it grates/irritates,' more negative/annoyed). Register: 신경 쓰여요 polite, 신경 쓰여 반말. The thing that bothers you takes 이/가: 그 말이 신경 쓰여요, not 그 말을.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 신경(nerves/attention) + 쓰이다(get used, passive of 쓰다) = 'my nerves are spent on it (involuntarily).' The real meaning: something occupies your mind without you choosing — a mild, involuntary preoccupation, like a tune you can't stop humming. Not full worry.

Use with friends, family, close coworkers when sharing what's been on your mind. 신경 쓰여요 is polite; 신경 쓰여 is 반말. 신경 쓰지 마세요 is the polite release phrase and can be used with anyone. Don't use it in formal complaints or official contexts — describe the issue neutrally there.

vs. 걱정돼요: future-oriented anxiety about an outcome ('I'm worried it might go wrong'). vs. 거슬리다: 'it grates/irritates me' — more negative and annoyed. vs. 귀찮다: 'it's a hassle, I can't be bothered' — laziness frame. vs. 불안하다: 'I feel anxious' — deeper unease. 신경 쓰이다 = neutral, mid-strength involuntary preoccupation.

신경 쓰여요 (polite passive), 신경 쓰지 마세요 (don't worry about it), 신경 쓰여서 잠이 안 와요 ('it's on my mind and I can't sleep'), 신경 쓰인다 (self-exclamation). Active partner: 제가 신경 쓸게요 ('I'll take care of it'). Cause takes 이/가: 그 말이 신경 쓰여요.

(1) Confusing 신경 써요 (active: 'I pay attention/care') with 신경 쓰여요 (passive: 'it nags at me') — the voice reverses the meaning. (2) Marking the cause with 을/를: it's 그 말이 신경 쓰여요 (이/가), not 그 말을. (3) Translating 'bother' as 귀찮다 — 귀찮다 means 'it's a hassle / I can't be bothered (laziness),' a completely different feeling.

mistakes: Confusing 신경 써요 with 신경 쓰여요.
신경 써요 = 'I (actively) pay attention/care.' 신경 쓰여요 = 'it (passively) bothers me.' Different voice, different meaning. For 'it nags at me,' use 신경 쓰여요.
Translating 'it bothers me' as 귀찮아요.
귀찮다 = 'it's a hassle / I can't be bothered (lazy).' For 'it preoccupies/nags at me,' the word is 신경 쓰여요. They're different feelings.
Marking the cause with 을/를: 그 말을 신경 쓰여요.
With the passive 쓰이다, the thing takes 이/가: 그 말이 신경 쓰여요. (Only the active 신경(을) 쓰다 takes 을/를.)

english: It feels like too much / it puts pressure on me
usage: It feels like a lot / it's too much pressure
Polite; uneasy under expectation, attention, or over-generosity — the socially gracious way to decline or push back
반말, to a friend when something feels like too big a favor or too much attention
Reassuring someone not to feel burdened — constant kindness phrase in Korean
Isn't this putting pressure on you?
Checking whether your ask/gift is burdening someone — considerate, common in Korean social interaction
examples: 이렇게 비싼 선물은 좀 부담스러워요.
A gift this expensive feels like too much.
부담스럽다 to graciously push back on over-generosity; 좀 softens the refusal politely
A: 다 제가 낼게요! / B: 아니에요, 부담스러워요. 같이 내요.
A: I'll pay for everything! / B: No, that's too much. Let's split it.
A/B exchange: B uses 부담스러워요 to decline graciously without refusing bluntly — the Korean way to push back on excess generosity
편하게 생각하세요. 부담 갖지 마세요.
Take it easy — no pressure at all.
부담 갖지 마세요 to lift the weight off someone — a frequent phrase when making a request or invitation
nuance: 부담스러워요 (from 부담스럽다, built on 부담 '負擔, a burden/load') is a socially essential Korean feeling with no neat English word: the uneasy 'this is too much for me' you feel under heavy expectation, intense attention, or someone's over-generosity. A too-expensive gift, an overwhelming compliment, everyone staring, a favor so large you'll feel perpetually indebted — all 부담스럽다. The thread is 'I feel weighed down / put on the spot, and I'd rather you dial it back.' It is polite and relational, often used to graciously DECLINE or soften: 부담스러우면 안 하셔도 돼요 ('if it's too much, you don't have to'). The key partner phrases are 부담(을) 주다 ('to burden/pressure someone else') and 부담(을) 갖다 ('to feel pressured'), so 부담 갖지 마세요 ('no pressure') is a constant kindness. Distinguish from 어렵다 (when a person feels intimidating, e.g., a strict boss — a social hierarchy feeling, not about weight of obligation) and 무겁다 (literally 'heavy'). Register: 부담스러워요 polite, 부담스러워 반말. The English-speaker pitfall is (1) having no word for it and bluntly refusing where a Korean would say 부담스러워요; (2) the -스럽다 irregular: 부담스럽다 → 부담스러워요 (ㅂ-irregular), not 부담해요 or 부담있어요; (3) mixing up 부담 주다 ('to burden someone') with 부담스럽다 ('I feel burdened').

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 부담(負擔, burden/load) + 스럽다(feels/seems like) = 'it has the quality of a burden.' The real social meaning: 'this is too much for me — I'm weighed down by the expectation or generosity, and I'd like you to dial it back.' It is also a polite, gracious way to decline, not a direct refusal.

Use with friends, family, coworkers — appropriate in most registers because it is polite and relational. 부담스러워요 is the polite form; 부담스러워 is 반말. Fine even to say to elders or in semi-formal contexts: 좀 부담스럽네요. The phrase 부담 갖지 마세요 is universally applicable as a kindness.

vs. 부담스럽다 vs. 어렵다: 어렵다 about a person means they feel intimidating/hard to approach (a hierarchy feeling), while 부담스럽다 is about the weight of obligation/expectation. vs. 무겁다: literally heavy (physical objects); 부담스럽다 is social/emotional weight. vs. 압박감을 느껴요: 'I feel pressured' — more formal, less conversational.

부담스럽네요 (softer observation), 부담 갖지 마세요 (reassurance), 부담 주려는 건 아닌데 ('I don't mean to pressure you, but...'), 부담이 돼요 ('it becomes a burden to me'), 부담 드리고 싶지 않아요 ('I don't want to burden you' — polite humble form). The ㅂ-irregular: 부담스럽다 → 부담스러워요.

(1) Having no equivalent word and bluntly refusing ('no, too expensive') — a Korean softens with 부담스러워요 to decline graciously. (2) Wrong form: 부담스럽다 → 부담스러워요 (ㅂ-irregular); 부담해요 and 부담있어요 are wrong. (3) Confusing 부담 주다 ('I am burdening someone') with 부담스럽다 ('I feel burdened') — the giver/receiver distinction matters.

mistakes: Bluntly refusing instead of softening with 부담스러워요.
To decline a big gift/favor graciously, Koreans say 좀 부담스러워요 ('it's a bit much for me'). A flat 'no, too expensive' is harsher; 부담스럽다 keeps it polite and relational.
Saying 부담해요 or 부담있어요.
The adjective is 부담스럽다 → 부담스러워요 (ㅂ-irregular). There's no 부담하다 for this feeling, and 부담있어요 isn't natural. Use 부담스러워요.
Confusing 부담 주다 with 부담스럽다.
부담 주다 = 'to pressure/burden someone (else)'; 부담스럽다 = 'I feel pressured/burdened.' 'You're pressuring me' = 부담스러워요 / 부담 주지 마세요, not 부담스러워 주세요.
